newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK C.BANK INTRODUCES REPO TENDER TO CURB LOANS.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK C.BANK INTRODUCES REPO TENDER TO CURB LOANS.

text.p: The Slovak central bank, hoping to curb lending by local banks, said on Tuesday it would hold tenders for short-term securities repurchase, a move analysts said would further spur already high interest rates.

National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) officials said the central bank had stopped quoting securities repurchase and reverse repo rates, instead opting to hold tenders to more closely regulate liquidity and help sterilise the money supply.

Analysts said the move would most likely have the desired effect, slowing local banks' recent penchance for extending mainly consumer-oriented credits, since interest rates may rise sharply in reaction.

"The banks' liquidity shortage is not pressing yet, though it should push the interbank interest rates gradually higher, by a maximum 50 basis points a day for a short while," Jozef Bozek, Tatra Banka chief dealer, said.

Added Martin Hrozanyi, chief dealer at Slovenska Sporitelna: "The central bank may succeed curbing the loan expansion now, because if a bank is to extend a loan today it would be at the Bratislava Interbank Offer Rate (BRIBOR) rate, and no firm will take a loan for (as high as) 16 percent."
BRIBOR overnight funds on Tuesday averaged 14.85 percent, up from 14.58 percent on the previous trading day. The three-month BRIBOR rate stood at 16.02 percent on Tuesday.

Peter Andresic, a head of the NBS's newly established Open Market Operation Department, told Reuters that the new system would take away the "automatic" possibility for banks to square their positions through the central bank.

He said the tenders will act as a short-term drainage instrument -- up to seven days for the time being -- focused on volumes exclusively, not interbank interest rates, which he said "will probably fluctuate significantly at first".
"We will not fix the rate, and if we will fix anything, it will be the volume when we supply liquidity," Andresic said.
The tenders are to be held at 1000 CET, with results released at 1100 CET and allocations following later in a day.
The NBS decided on Tuesday not to hold a tender, as current liquidity in the banking sector did not warrant intervention, Andresic said.
Tender announcements will include the type of tender -- refinancing or sterilising -- and its style -- American or Dutch. In case the tender is refinancing, the NBS would also fix a specific volume.

Any Slovak bank or Slovak branch of a foreign bank can bid with "any security" in the repo tender, Andresic said adding it was possibile the NBS would also hold individual repo trades or direct trades with banks along with, or after, tenders.

"(But) our activity is turning interventionist, and we will intervene on the money supply growth...assuming that mainly by reducing refinancing volumes, we would help to reduce banks credit activities," Andresic said.

In 1996, Slovak banks markedly increased their lending activities, pushing the key money supply measure, M2, 19.0 percent year-on-year by September. The NBS full-year target was an expansion of 11.6 percent year-on-year.

Most dealers agree with Andresic that credit activities will be curtailed, saying the uncertainty created by the central bank move should tighten liquidity by taking away refinancing opportunities and making banks wary of opening new positions.
"Refinancing possibilities for banks are no longer as certain (as they used to be), and even if there is, refinancing will be very, very expensive," Hrozanyi said.
Added Pavol Kruk of Istrobanka: "Questionable are mainly one-to-three month maturities quotations, no one knows what to expect now, and thus banks appear reluctant to open positions."
